title: Molecular characterization and phylogenetic analysis of the
abstract: Marek's disease (MD) is a highly contagious lymphoproliferative disease of chickens caused by Marek's disease virus serotype 1 (MDV-1) and remains a major concern for the global poultry industry despite widespread vaccination. Although current vaccines effectively prevent clinical disease, the emergence of more virulent strains has been recorded. Molecular surveillance of field strains is essential, particularly in regions where data remain limited. This study aimed to molecularly characterize MDV-1 isolates from recent cases in Vietnamese commercial poultry flocks, focusing on the meq gene, a key virulence-associated marker, and to compare variants with vaccine strains CVI988/Rispens. A total of 12 MDV-1 positive samples from multiple regions of Vietnam were analyzed using Sanger sequencing of the full-length meq gene. Phylogenetic analysis grouped the Vietnamese isolates into three genetic clusters (G1-G3). The attenuated-like G1 isolates showed high similarity to CVI988/Rispens clones and contained four to seven proline-rich repeat (PPPP) motifs. In contrast, G2 and G3 isolates were classified as field virulent genotypes and contained two to three PPPP motifs. Comparative sequence analysis revealed multiple amino-acid substitutions in the Meq protein relative to CVI988/Rispens, including conserved mutations characteristic of Asian field strains. Vietnamese isolates clustered primarily with contemporary Asian lineages from China and India. The results demonstrate the presence of both vaccine-derived and virulent MDV-1 strains in this Vietnamese sample set and highlight the importance of continued molecular surveillance to monitor viral evolution and support vaccination strategies.

title: The Journey of Newcastle Disease Virus Across the Indonesian Archipelago.
abstract: Newcastle disease (ND), caused by Newcastle disease virus (NDV), remains a major threat to poultry production, food security, and livelihoods worldwide. ND was first recognized in Java, Indonesia, in 1926, followed by its description in Newcastle-upon-Tyne, England, in 1927. Since then, ND has been repeatedly detected in Indonesian poultry systems, including free-range, backyard, and commercial production, with outbreaks causing substantial mortality and economic losses. Indonesia's archipelagic geography, extensive poultry movement and marketing networks, and heterogeneous production systems create complex conditions for virus persistence and dissemination. This review summarizes the century-long journey (1926-2026) of NDV in Indonesia, highlighting its historical emergence, epidemiological evolution, genetic diversity, and control strategies. Molecular epidemiological studies demonstrate substantial genetic diversity, with virulent genotype VII viruses frequently associated with contemporary outbreaks, while genotypes I, II, VI, and XIII have also been reported in Indonesian domestic and wild birds. The evidence supports repeated endemic circulation and ongoing viral evolution across Indonesia, emphasizing the importance of continuous molecular surveillance to monitor viral diversity and inform control strategies. Understanding the long-term epidemiological and evolutionary dynamics of NDV in Indonesia provides valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying viral emergence and persistence in a unique geographical location. Strengthening representative genomic surveillance, improving vaccination implementation, and enhancing regional cooperation across Southeast Asia will be critical for mitigating the future impact of ND on poultry production and food security.

title: Global Virology Meets the Viruses of the Changing World: Where Ecology, Evolution, One Health, Artificial Intelligence, and Innovation Unite to Decode Viruses.
abstract: This article highlights the current issue of VirusDisease in the fast-changing scenario of modern virology and introduces the VIROCON 2026, the flagship national conference of the Indian Virological Society, which will be held in Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala, on 11-13 November 2026 with the theme "Viruses in the ChangingWorld: Ecology, Evolution and Future Preparedness." The current issue covers the wide range of contemporary virological research, including molecular and structural virology, emerging and re-emerging viruses, diagnostics, computational methods, epidemiology, co-infections, and viral evolution. VIROCON 2026 builds on this interdisciplinary perspective with eight thematic tracks that combine One Health, AI, metagenomics, ecology, climate change, therapeutics, vaccines, and preparedness. The issue and conference highlight the need for collaboration, innovation, and globally connected virology to prepare for and address future viral threats.

title: Detection of novel Echovirus 25 lineage from patients and sewage in Fukuoka in 2024.
abstract: Echovirus 25 (E25), belonging to the Enterovirus B species of viruses, is known to cause infectious gastroenteriris, aseptic meningitis, and acute flaccid paralysis. Our study aims to conduct enterovirus surveillance and subsequent molecular epidemiology investigations among patients and sewage samples in Fukuoka. In 2024, a total of ten and seven enteroviral strains were detected in 141 clinical specimens and 24 sewage samples, respectively. Among them, five E25 strains were identified, and phylogenetic analysis of VP1 region revealed that these strains constituted a distinct clade separated from previously reported E25 strains. Full-length genome sequences were determined using sequence-independent, single-primer amplification and next-generation sequencing. The five strains had sequence identities ranging from 99.0% to 99.9% among themselves. Through phylogenetic analysis, the five strains were classified as E25 on the basis of P1, and P1-3 sequences, and as E3 and E11 on the basis of P2-3 sequence. Furthermore, SimPlot and RDP4 analysis revealed a unique recombination event between the detected E25 strains and E3 in the region of the 2B gene, which is the non-structural region. These findings indicated the emergence of a novel E25 lineage in 2024, and underscore the importance of continued surveillance to monitor its evolution and circulation.

title: A Single-Reaction Multiplex PCR Assay for Rapid Screening and Epidemiological Analysis of Hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae.
abstract: Hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae (HvKp) causes invasive infections, and rapid clone estimation and virulence gene detection are important for treatment and infection control. We modified a previously developed PCR-based open reading frame typing (POT) method and developed HvKp-POT, a single-reaction 13-plex PCR assay for simultaneous clone estimation and detection of hypervirulence-associated genes. The assay includes a K. pneumoniae marker, six ORFs for clone estimation, and targets for K1, K2, iucA, iroB, rmpA/A2, and peg-344. We validated the assay using 106 genome-analyzed Klebsiella strains, including 44 HvKp strains. POT results were expressed as HvKp-POT-1 for clone estimation, and HvKp-POT-2 for virulence gene detection. HvKp-POT-1 values corresponded to major HvKp clones and showed one-to-one concordance with sequence types in 75 of 95 K. pneumoniae strains. Strains with the same POT-1 value sometimes included both HvKp and classical K. pneumoniae, but these were generally distinguished using HvKp-POT-2. HvKp-POT may be useful for rapid HvKp screening and epidemiological analysis.

title: Genomic Characterization of Blood-Derived Non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae in the Kinki Region of Japan Using Whole-Genome Sequencing.
abstract: Non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae (NTHi)-related invasive disease and antimicrobial resistance are emerging public health concerns, but genomic data on domestic isolates remain limited. We performed a genomic epidemiological analysis of 15 H. influenzae strains isolated from blood samples (n=15) at seven participating medical institutions in the Kinki region of Japan between 2018 and 2020. Whole-genome sequencing with hybrid assembly showed that all isolates were NTHi. Multilocus sequence typing identified 10 sequence types, including recurrent ST165 and ST107, and core-genome single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) analysis revealed three clusters, while unclustered strains showed high genetic diversity. Additional pan-genome and Virulence Factor Database (VFDB)-based analyses showed heterogeneous distribution of putative virulence-associated genes, particularly those related to adhesion, iron/heme acquisition, and lipooligosaccharide or outer-membrane structures. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing showed that 73.3% of isolates were phenotypically classified as β-lactamase-negative ampicillin-resistant (BLNAR), while penicillin-binding protein 3 (PBP3) mutation analysis showed that 73.3% were genotypically classified as high-gBLNAR. One ST422 isolate showed reduced susceptibility to moxifloxacin and carried gyrA S84L and parC S84I substitutions. These findings provide regional baseline data on the genomic diversity, resistance mechanisms, and molecular epidemiology of invasive NTHi in the Kinki region of Japan.

title: Molecular epidemiology of Theileria parva in Eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo: implications for the introduction of the Muguga cocktail vaccine against East Coast Fever.
abstract: East Coast Fever (ECF) is one of the most economically important tick-borne diseases of cattle in Eastern, Central, and Southern Africa, caused by the intracellular protozoan parasite Theileria parva (T. parva). This study investigated the seroprevalence and genetic diversity of T. parva populations in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to inform immunization strategies against ECF. A cross-sectional study was conducted between September 2012 and January 2013 in three provinces of eastern DRC (North Kivu, South Kivu, and Ituri) to assess the seroprevalence and confirm the presence of T. parva in cattle. Blood samples from 31 villages across different agro-ecological zones were analyzed using the PIM ELISA, and ELISA-positive samples were further screened by p104 PCR. An immunization and field challenge trial using the Muguga cocktail vaccine was conducted with 100 seronegative cattle. Molecular characterization of samples collected from the sentinel, immunized, and control groups was performed by sequencing the p67, Tp1, and Tp2 genes and conducting microsatellite genotyping. Data were analyzed using MEGA, DnaSP, GenAIEx, FSTAT, and LIAN to determine genetic variation, population structure, and linkage equilibrium among T. parva isolates. Of the 756 serum samples analyzed, 27.5% tested positive for T. parva antibodies by ELISA, with Ituri showing the highest seroprevalence and North Kivu the lowest. PCR confirmed T. parva DNA in 87.5% of ELISA-positive samples. Sentinel cattle exposed in Kabasha village developed severe ECF, confirming high transmission pressure, and were used to establish the immunization and challenge site. Vaccination with the Muguga cocktail induced seroconversion in 94% of cattle, with 46.5% surviving field challenge. Sequence analysis of p67, Tp1, and Tp2 genes revealed limited clustering with Muguga strains and high polymorphism, particularly in Tp2 (13.2%). Microsatellite genotyping detected substantial allelic diversity and population sub-structuring, with unique alleles predominant across loci (Fst = 0.118). This study revealed high and variable T. parva seroprevalence across eastern DRC, with genetic analyses indicating the coexistence of Muguga-like and distinct local parasite populations. The low survival rate in immunized cattle highlights limitations of the Muguga cocktail against field strains. These findings highlight the presence of diverse T. parva populations and emphasize the need for continuous genetic monitoring and tailored vaccine strategies to enhance ECF control in the region.

title: Molecular Epidemiology and Spatial Distribution of Toxocara canis and Toxocara cati in Avian Paratenic Hosts: A One Health Perspective From Northeastern Iran.
abstract: Toxocara canis and Toxocara cati are zoonotic nematodes, and birds may contribute to their transmission as paratenic hosts. Data on their molecular occurrence in avian hosts remain limited in northeastern Iran. This study investigated the molecular detection and spatial distribution of T. canis and T. cati in synanthropic and domestic birds from Razavi Khorasan Province. In this cross-sectional study, 300 tissue samples (brain, eye and liver) were collected from 100 birds: sparrows (n = 60), pigeons (n = 21) and chickens (n = 19). Detection and species identification were performed using multiplex nested PCR targeting ITS regions. Spatial patterns were assessed using kernel density estimation and Global Moran's I in ArcGIS 10.8. Associated factors were analysed by multivariable mixed-effects logistic regression. Toxocara spp. DNA was detected in 51/300 tissues (17.0%) and 35/100 birds (35.0%). Tissue-level positivity was highest in sparrows (23.3%), followed by chickens (8.8%) and pigeons (6.3%). In sparrows, detection differed among tissues (p = 0.026), with higher positivity in eye and liver. T. canis predominated (68.6%), followed by mixed infections (17.7%) and T. cati (13.7%). Bird species and tissue type were independently associated with PCR positivity. Kernel Density Estimation suggested localised southern and southeastern hotspots, whereas Global Moran's I showed a non-significant random spatial pattern. Synanthropic and domestic birds, particularly sparrows, may act as paratenic hosts for Toxocara spp. in northeastern Iran. Higher detection in eye and liver tissues suggests zoonotic relevance, especially through undercooked poultry giblets; however, DNA detection does not confirm larval viability.

title: Design and evaluation of probe-capture sequencing for clinical Neisseria gonorrhoeae specimens
abstract: Characterizing the molecular epidemiology of Neisseria gonorrhoeae is essential for understanding disease burden, elucidating transmission dynamics, and informing clinical decision-making and public health interventions. Given that routine, culture-independent diagnostics rapidly and sensitively detect this difficult-to-cultivate pathogen, aligning genomic surveillance with these workflows is necessary to understand its epidemiology and evolutionary dynamics. To address this challenge, we investigated the utility of probe-capture sequencing to selectively enrich for pathogen-specific DNA during next-generation sequencing. Custom biotinylated oligonucleotide baits were designed using genetic information from publicly available genomes hosted on Pathogenwatch. Of the 32,574 assemblies, 2,877 representative genomes were selected to inform probe generation using core genome amino acid distance clustering and representation of unique resistance-associated genotypes and predicted resistance phenotypes. The resulting probe set provided generous coverage of the reference genome, N. gonorrhoeae FA 1090, with 94.6% nucleotide coverage and 99.3% of annotated genes covered by at least one probe. Piloting this technology on 12 clinical urine specimens with variable relative pathogen abundances revealed that probe-capture sequencing substantially increased the relative abundance of N. gonorrhoeae sequence reads from a complex sample (fold-change range, 226 - 2046), enabling considerable genome coverage, the construction of high-quality genome assemblies, and the detection of resistance-associated genotypes. These findings demonstrate that probe-capture sequencing is a viable method for enriching N. gonorrhoeae genetic material from clinical samples, enabling culture-independent genomic investigations into the epidemiology of hard-to-culture pathogens and providing actionable insights to inform clinical and public health interventions.
